method_note: FAST mode, one round. F-001 to F-019 reused from articles/2026-11-17-bali-wedding-packages/02-research-B.json, keeping original checked dates; source_ref gives the original ID. New facts from F-100.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia: 'Generally, Indonesian nationals, and persons of any other nationality may marry in Indonesia provided they hold a religion recognised by the Indonesian Government (Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism or Christian). Under the Indonesian Marriage Law, marriages may be performed by Ministers of Religion, officers of the Civil Registry Office (Kantor Catatan Sipil) or the Office of Religious Affairs (Kantor Urusan Agama). For a marriage to be legal, it must be conducted according to the religion and conform to the laws of the countries of the parties involved.'
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Quote as the Embassy's 'general guide only'. The religion list is the Embassy's short form; see new facts for the Indonesian official position. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office (Catatan Sipil) where the marriage takes place, or the Indonesian Embassy or Consulate-General in Australia.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia, 'Couples must be of the same religion': 'Under Indonesian Law No.1 of 1974 concerning marriage (the 'Marriage Law'), both parties must hold the same religion, if not, one party must convert to the other religion.'
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: This is the Embassy's reading of the law; the statute itself does not use the words 'same religion' (see F-1xx on art. 2(1)). Quote it as the Embassy's wording. Do not repeat the Embassy's 'anecdotal' remark about conversion. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office and the Australian Consulate-General Bali.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia, Other Weddings: for non-Muslim marriages (Christian, Hindu, etc.), couples lodge a Notice of Intention to Marry with the Civil Registry Office at least 10 days before the wedding; after the ceremony the marriage must be registered at the Civil Registry Office to be legal. Both applicants need originals and photocopies of: the CNI from the Embassy or Consulate-General; passports or KTP; birth certificates; marriage certificate; proof of dissolution of a previous marriage or death certificate of a former partner (if applicable); four photos (4x6cm) of the couple. Requirements can vary from province to province, so check with the Civil Registry Office where you will marry first.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: 'Marriage certificate' appears in the list as written; its meaning is unclear (likely the religious certificate), so say 'the documents your Civil Registry Office lists'. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office (Dinas Kependudukan dan Pencatatan Sipil) of the regency where you marry.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia, Islamic Weddings: Muslim weddings are performed by the Office of Religious Affairs (Kantor Urusan Agama), which issues the Marriage Book (Buku Nikah) as evidence of the marriage. There is usually no requirement to register such a marriage with the Civil Registry Office, but a Civil Registry Marriage Certificate is recommended if you intend to relocate to another country.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Confirmed by the local KUA.

facts.claim: Indonesia (including Bali): an Australian marrying in Indonesia applies for a Certificate of No Impediment (CNI) from the Australian Embassy in Jakarta or a Consulate-General; Bali, NTB and NTT fall under the Australian Consulate-General in Bali. The local Civil Registry Office or KUA normally requires the CNI from the mission with jurisdiction.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Confirmed by the Australian Consulate-General Bali and the Civil Registry Office where the marriage will take place.

facts.claim: Indonesia: 'We do not place an expiry date on the CNI, however the local Civil Registry Office do not normally accept CNIs that were issued more than 3 months prior.'
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Civil Registry practice, not law; confirm with the Civil Registry Office in the regency where you marry.

facts.claim: Indonesia: for non-Muslim marriages, couples lodge a Notice of Intention to Marry with the Civil Registry Office at least 10 days before the wedding, and the marriage must be registered there afterwards to be legal. Both parties must hold the same religion recognised by the Indonesian Government (Law No. 1 of 1974). A CNI is usually issued while you wait if documents are complete.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: The Embassy calls this 'a general guide only'. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office in the area of the wedding.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia FAQ: you cannot marry at the Embassy or Consulate-General; a CNI is usually issued while you wait if documents are correct and complete; since 1 January 1995 any legally performed overseas marriage that would have been legal in Australia is accepted as a legal marriage under Australian law; you do not register the marriage with the Embassy, and cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia; you cannot marry before a divorce decree absolute is issued.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Confirmed by the Australian Consulate-General Bali.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Indonesia: 'Neither DFAT nor its missions overseas can advise on other countries' specific requirements for Australians to get married overseas.' For current requirements contact the nearest Indonesian Embassy or Consulate-General or the Indonesian Civil Registry Office (Catatan Sipil) where the marriage will take place. Couples make their own arrangements with the religious minister and/or civil registry celebrants, and are advised to talk to a lawyer in Australia and/or Indonesia. The Embassy suggests engaging a Wedding Organiser if unsure.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Indonesia (DFAT), Marriage in Indonesia
facts.use_note: Do not imply the Embassy endorses any organiser.

facts.claim: You cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia. Australia does not recognise overseas marriages where either person was already married, not old enough, too closely related, or forced to marry. A foreign marriage certificate may not be usable as proof of a name change; check with your state or territory BDM registry.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Getting married overseas
facts.use_note: Confirmed by DFAT; for name change use, the state or territory BDM registry.

facts.claim: The Attorney-General's Department says overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised marriage celebrant or registered in Australia, and an overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was valid in the overseas country and would have been valid here. Legal basis: Marriage Act 1961, Part VA.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: A Bali ceremony led by an Australian celebrant is symbolic unless the Indonesian legal process is also followed.

facts.claim: Legal at home, celebration abroad: Australia has no marriage licence; the formal step is giving a Notice of Intended Marriage (NOIM) to an authorised celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding. Since 12 June 2024 the NOIM can be witnessed remotely by audio-visual link, and a couple outside Australia can complete it with an authorised witness overseas (such as an Australian consular officer or a notary public, not a celebrant).
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: Present as an option, not advice: legal ceremony in Australia, symbolic ceremony in Bali.

facts.claim: Since 12 June 2024 the authorised celebrant must meet separately and in person with each party before the marriage, and must be physically present to solemnise it, together with the couple and 2 witnesses over 18. There are no video-link weddings.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married

facts.claim: How to apply for a CNI through DFAT: complete the CNI application form, signing it only in front of an authorised witness. DFAT advises checking whether the CNI must be issued in the country of marriage, in which case the Australian embassy there can issue it.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage

facts.claim: DFAT notarial fees from 1 January 2026, in Australian dollars: Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage AUD 181; document legalisation by Apostille AUD 105. Fees rise with CPI on 1 January each year.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Notarial services
facts.use_note: Write 'from AUD 181 (2026 DFAT fee)' for a CNI issued in Australia. Fee at the Consulate-General Bali not read.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Indonesia: Indonesia's revised criminal code includes penalties for cohabitation, adultery and sex outside of marriage between a man and a woman. If you're married, authorities can act on a complaint from your spouse; if you're unmarried, authorities can act on a complaint from your child or parent.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Indonesia travel advice
facts.use_note: Optional context; state exactly as worded.

facts.claim: Australian Consulate-General, Bali, Jalan Tantular 32, Renon, Denpasar Bali 80234; phone (+62 361) 2000 100; website bali.indonesia.embassy.gov.au.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Indonesia travel advice
facts.use_note: Mission with CNI jurisdiction for Bali (F-005). Prefer linking.

facts.claim: Constitutional Court of Indonesia, official Summary of Decision for case 24/PUU-XX/2022, 'Legitimacy and Registration of Interfaith Marriages': judicial review of Article 2 paragraphs (1) and (2) and Article 8 letter f of Law 1/1974. 'Verdict: To dismiss the Petitioner's petition entirely.' Date of decision: Tuesday, January 31, 2023. The Court states it 'remains in its stance on the constitutionality of valid marriages, which are those carried out according to their religion and belief and that every marriage must be registered in accordance with statutory regulations.'
facts.publisher: Constitutional Court of the Republic of Indonesia (Mahkamah Konstitusi), English summary of decision
facts.use_note: Deciding authority: Constitutional Court. English summary is the Court's own translation; quote neutrally. The summary also cites earlier decisions 46/PUU-VIII/2010 and 68/PUU-XII/2014 on the same article.

facts.claim: Constitutional Court summary, 24/PUU-XX/2022, quoting its earlier decisions 46/PUU-VIII/2010 and 68/PUU-XII/2014: 'the validity of a marriage is a religious domain through religious institutions or organizations that are authorized or have the authority to provide religious interpretations. The state's role, in this case, is to follow up on the results of the interpretation given by the religious institution or organization.' And: 'religion determines the validity of marriage and at the same time the state determines the administrative validity of marriage within the legal corridor.'
facts.publisher: Constitutional Court of the Republic of Indonesia (Mahkamah Konstitusi)
facts.use_note: This is the clearest official explanation of why validity depends on religion. It means each couple's religious authority, not the state, decides whether their marriage is religiously valid. Do not paraphrase as 'Indonesia bans' anything; quote.

facts.claim: Article 2 paragraph (1) of Law No. 1 of 1974 on Marriage, as quoted by the Constitutional Court (English): 'A marriage shall be legitimate if it is performed according to the laws of the respective religions and beliefs of the parties concerned.' Indonesian text as quoted by the Court: 'perkawinan adalah sah apabila dilakukan menurut hukum masing-masing agama dan kepercayaannya itu'. Article 2(2) requires every marriage to be registered according to statutory regulations.
facts.publisher: Constitutional Court of the Republic of Indonesia, news (English version; Indonesian original at mkri.id/berita/larangan-perkawinan-beda-agama-dianggap-diskriminatif-24082 prevails)
facts.use_note: Medium only because the statute text itself on peraturan.bpk.go.id returned HTTP 503 today (N-100); wording is as quoted by the Court. Art. 2(2) wording is from the 24/PUU-XX/2022 summary (F-100), not a direct statute read. The same page records Justice Ridwan Mansyur referring to 'Law No. 1 of 1974 as amended by Law No. 16 of 2019'; the 2019 amendment's content was not read.

facts.claim: Constitutional Court summary, 24/PUU-XX/2022: 'Article 34 of Law Number 23 of 2006 concerning Population Administration ... as amended by Law Number 24 of 2013 ... confirms that every citizen who has entered into a marriage which is legal according to statutory regulations has the right to register their marriage at the civil registry office for non-Muslim couples and at the Office of Religious Affairs (Kantor Urusan Agama or KUA) for Muslim couples.'
facts.publisher: Constitutional Court of the Republic of Indonesia (Mahkamah Konstitusi)
facts.use_note: Official basis for 'KUA for Muslim couples, Civil Registry (Dukcapil) for non-Muslim couples'. Matches the Australian Embassy (F-003, F-004). Population Administration Law text not read directly (N-101).

facts.claim: Constitutional Court summary, 24/PUU-XX/2022, on Article 35 letter a of Law 23/2006: 'Although the elucidation of Article 35 letter a of Law 23/2006 describes that what is meant by marriage determined by a court is a marriage between people of different religions, the Court is of the opinion that it does not necessarily mean that the state recognizes interfaith marriages because the state, in this case, follows the interpretation that has been carried out by religious institutions or organizations'. The Court calls court-determined registration 'a regulation in the field of population administration' because validity 'still has to refer to the norms of Article 2 paragraph (1) of Law 1/1974'.
facts.publisher: Constitutional Court of the Republic of Indonesia (Mahkamah Konstitusi)
facts.use_note: Explains the court-registration route under Article 35 and the Court's view of it. Read with F-105 (SEMA 2/2023), which tells courts not to grant such applications.

facts.claim: Indonesia: Government Regulation (PP) No. 9 of 1975, implementing Marriage Law No. 1 of 1974, article 10: following the procedure of each religion or belief, the marriage takes place before the Registrar (Pegawai Pencatat) and is attended by two witnesses ('dihadiri oleh dua orang saksi').
facts.publisher: Badan Pemeriksa Keuangan RI (Indonesian Audit Board) legal database
facts.use_note: Medium: confirmed via search excerpts, not read in full. Confirmed by the Civil Registry Office in Bali.
